items.title: [tornado] Tornado: Event loop blocking and excess memory use from chunked bodies with many small chunks
items.summary: SummaryWhen Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default max_body_size of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use @stream_request_body stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.ImpactAll Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering max_body_size reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.SimpleAsyncHTTPClient is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.PatchesFixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to data_received, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.Applications using @stream_request_body should note that the pieces passed to data_received no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.WorkaroundsRun Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a Content-Length header instead of chunked encoding.Lower max_body_size (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.CreditReported by uttej-badwane.Referenceshttps://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/security/advisories/GHSA-r4j5-9xpp-3985https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115927https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/pull/3773https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/ceab33581489751a66fba8566ad6d5960d4b01c8https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/releases/tag/v6.6.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r4j5-9xpp-3985

items.title: [tornado] Tornado: Open redirect in RedirectHandler via protocol-relative URLs
items.summary: Summarytornado.web.RedirectHandler builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.ImpactApplications are affected if they use RedirectHandler with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:A substitution at the start of the path, for example (r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"}). A request to https://example.com//evil.com/target redirects to //evil.com/destination, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to //.A substitution directly after the host, for example (r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"}). A request to /old.evil.com/ or /old@evil.com/ redirects to evil.com.A template that begins with a substitution (such as "{0}"), which can be given an absolute URL.Applications are not affected if their RedirectHandler templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a / (for example "/static/{0}" or "https://example.com/{0}"). Other uses of RequestHandler.redirect() are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to redirect() should validate it themselves.PatchesFixed in Tornado 6.6. RedirectHandler now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in StaticFileHandler has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.WorkaroundsChange RedirectHandler templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in /, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as /, \, @, . or : where they could affect the host.Alternatively, replace RedirectHandler with a custom handler that validates the target before calling self.redirect().CreditReported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).Referenceshttps://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/security/advisories/GHSA-pw9p-v7r6-gx4phttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116578https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/pull/3786https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/940ea725bdd9bc68231d68a105eef17ea6e11233https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/cc75ab0eb3af459c714895a49f682ad354f50117https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/ccb6a2e5482f17997efd4a74b8200d5b4babc035https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/releases/tag/v6.6.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pw9p-v7r6-gx4p

items.title: [tornado] Tornado: Quadratic CPU usage when parsing HTTP headers with line folding
items.summary: SummaryTornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.ImpactAll Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.How bad it gets depends on max_header_size:Default (64 KB): each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service.Raised max_header_size: the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.PatchesFixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.WorkaroundsKeep max_header_size at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it.Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.CreditReported by @manus-pi.Referenceshttps://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/security/advisories/GHSA-pcg2-g6cj-q92chttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116577https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/pull/3765https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/1b7a1dc9f340f52de929852e8125aa12f25297c9https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/releases/tag/v6.6.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pcg2-g6cj-q92c

items.title: [electrum] Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
items.summary: SummaryThe main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented design. [0]However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,and update the client's history with a conflicting (invalid) tx2 that replaces the outputs with the attacker's output address.Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.FixesCommit 90fe30822 contains the fix [1], included in version 4.8.3.The client now verifies the signatures of wallet.is_mine inputs for mempool txs (before adding them to its local history).Users should upgrade (and regularly do so in any case).As a workaround, without upgrading, when signing any transaction, for bumping the fee or not, they should verify the output addresses and amounts are as expected.Clients that connect to servers they trust (e.g. run their own) are not affected.Remarkssome servers are performing this attack in the wildelectrum received two user-reports of this. user1 noticed after broadcasting tx1 the wallet history contained a different tx. user2 bumped the fee of tx2 and lost money.user1 reported tx1 was not propagated over the bitcoin p2p, so the server held itboth reported the attacker's output address in tx2 was grinded to match the last four chars of the legit address from tx1based on user2's report, the server constructed a tx2 with zero fee (presumably in hope of the user bumping its fee)even with the fix, we still only validate "is_mine" inputs (i.e. paying from addresses that the wallet owns). So e.g. "incoming" txs are not validated. The client lacks a full consensus engine / script interpreter, though even with that, to cover non-is_mine inputs, it would have to validate the unconfirmed parents recursively until reaching mined txs. Mined txs we already SPV.Timeline2026-10-11: user1 sends private disclosure, but the bump_fee vector is not realised2026-10-18: user2 (Raju-K12) reports privately that they lost money after bump_fee2026-10-23: version 4.8.3 git tagged, with the fix2026-10-24: version 4.8.3 binaries released2026-10-24: public disclosureCreditsElectrum thanks user1 and Raju-K12 for finding and responsibly disclosing this issue to us.Referenceshttps://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/security/advisories/GHSA-6jp4-8v48-cc5vhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-117601https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/commit/90fe30822561e515a9d2d6e5a352cc07780999ebhttps://www.binance.com/en/square/post/381361716824742https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/electrum-before-4.8.3-missing-signature-verification-of-mempool-transactionshttps://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6jp4-8v48-cc5v

items.title: [mem0ai] Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
items.summary: Summary_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:def _build_session_scope(filters):    parts = []    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):        val = filters.get(key)        if val:            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")    return "&".join(parts)_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).ImpactAny caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id= (or &agent_id=) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).Reproductionfrom mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scopeTenant A: real user_id + run_idscope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"})print(scope_a)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside itscope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"})print(scope_c)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"assert scope_a == scope_c  # byte-for-byte collisionA full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.Suggested FixReject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts,Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the samekey=value&key=value string with the delimiters unescaped:  private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string {    const parts: string[] = [];    for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) {      const val = (filters as any)[key];      if (val) parts.push(${key}=${val});    }    return parts.join("&");  }The scope string is used the same way, as an exact-match key into the messagestable via SQLiteManager.getLastMessages() and saveMessages(), so the identicalforge, cross-tenant read and eviction all apply.Verified against the current releases as of 2026-07-26: pip mem0ai v2.0.14 andnpm mem0ai ts-v3.1.2 both still contain the unescaped join.Reporter: Abhinav Singh (GitHub: OfficialAbhinavSingh)Referenceshttps://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/security/advisories/GHSA-5324-3w58-qpp2https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116575https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/pull/6892https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/commit/71f2ebefa3494da21550fb525216818776cde67fhttps://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/releases/tag/ts-v3.1.6https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/releases/tag/v2.0.18https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5324-3w58-qpp2

items.title: [social-auth-core] Python Social Auth: OpenID Connect nonce is not bound to the browser session, so a stolen authorization code logs the attacker in as the victim
items.summary: SummaryThe generic OpenID Connect backend (OpenIdConnectAuth and every backend built on it) stores the nonce in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, validate_claims only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. With social-auth-core, the attacker can. They start their own login to get a valid state for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's code and their own state. state passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. The attacker's browser is now logged in as the victim.PKCE would block this, but OpenIdConnectAuth sets DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False (the OAuth2 base class defaults to True), so the nonce is the only binding in the default setup.Tested versionssocial-auth-core 6.1.1 (latest), 6.1.0 and 5.2.0, with social-auth-app-django 7.1.0 and Django 6.1.2, Python 3.14. The same code is on master (098ef399c1).Detailssocial_core/backends/open_id_connect.py in 6.1.1:line 252: auth_params calls get_and_store_nonce(self.authorization_url(), state)lines 333 to 346: get_and_store_nonce stores the nonce as an OpenIdConnectAssociation keyed by server_url and handle=nonce. The state goes into assoc_type but is never read back.lines 348 to 358: get_nonce looks the nonce up by server_url and handle onlylines 393 to 415: validate_claims accepts any stored, unexpired nonce and removes itline 110: DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = FalsePoCEverything runs locally. mockidp.py is a small OpenID provider on 127.0.0.1 that checks redirect_uri and enforces PKCE when a code_challenge was sent, like a normal provider. social_nonce.py uses two Django test clients as two browsers.pip install social-auth-core social-auth-app-django django pyjwt cryptographypython social_nonce.pyOutput on 6.1.1:[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: (200, 'user=victim')Controls:MODE=control_victim python social_nonce.py[control] victim completes normally: (200, 'user=victim')MODE=control_unknown_nonce python social_nonce.py[control] unknown nonce: ('EXC', 'AuthResponseError: The authentication response could not be matched to the request.')PKCE=1 python social_nonce.py[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: ('EXC', 'AuthCredentialError: The authorization code was rejected. Please restart login.')So the nonce check runs, but it accepts a nonce that belongs to another browser. With PKCE on, the same attack fails.mockidp.py:"""Minimal local OpenID Provider on 127.0.0.1 for testing RP libraries."""import json, time, secrets, threading, hashlib, base64, urllib.parsefrom http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServerimport jwtfrom cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsadef b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()class IdP:    def __init__(self, port=0, client_id="rp-client", client_secret="rp-secret", name="idp"):        self.key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)        self.kid = name + "-k1"        self.client_id, self.client_secret = client_id, client_secret        self.codes = {}        self.access = {}        self.claims_override = {}        self.srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), self._handler())        self.port = self.srv.server_address[1]        self.issuer = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.port}"        threading.Thread(target=self.srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()    def jwk(self):        n = self.key.public_key().public_numbers()        tb = lambda i: i.to_bytes((i.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")        return {"kty": "RSA", "kid": self.kid, "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": b64u(tb(n.n)), "e": b64u(tb(n.e))}    def discovery(self):        i = self.issuer        return {"issuer": i, "authorization_endpoint": i + "/authorize", "token_endpoint": i + "/token",                "userinfo_endpoint": i + "/userinfo", "jwks_uri": i + "/jwks",                "response_types_supported": ["code"], "subject_types_supported": ["public"],                "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],                "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"],                "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"]}    def user_authorizes(self, authorize_url, sub):        """The end user `sub` approves an authorization request; returns (code, params)."""        q = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(urllib.parse.urlsplit(authorize_url).query))        code = "code-" + secrets.token_hex(8)        self.codes[code] = {"sub": sub, "nonce": q.get("nonce"), "redirect_uri": q.get("redirect_uri"),

items.title: [onnx] ONNX: Out-of-bounds read in ConvTranspose shape inference via undersized weight rank
items.summary: SummaryONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a kernel_shape attribute.The inference function derived an empty effective_kernel_shape vector from the undersized weight tensor, then indexed that vector once for each spatial dimension of the input tensor. A crafted model passed onnx.checker.check_model() and caused SIGSEGV when passed to onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes().Technical detailsFor an input shape such as [1, 1, 5], shape inference computes one spatial input dimension. A weight shape such as [1, 3] has no spatial dimensions, so deriving kernel_shape from dimensions 2 onward produces an empty vector. The output loop nevertheless accesses effective_kernel_shape[0].The defect affected both the older convTransposeShapeInference_opset11() path and the then-current ConvTranspose inference implementation.ImpactAn application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. The observed result was a deterministic process crash. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.Affected versionsAffected: ONNX 1.2.1 through 1.21.0Patched: ONNX 1.22.0RemediationUpgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix rejects input and weight tensors with fewer than three dimensions before deriving the spatial kernel shape.Fix: onnx/onnx#7997Commit: 2ec288908The original malformed model was re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises InferenceError.SeverityThe vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.Referenceshttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/security/advisories/GHSA-6pwm-x34p-fvj2https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115920https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7997https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/2ec288908952eea9dcf48d4b197915e1f72c6abfhttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/releases/tag/v1.22.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6pwm-x34p-fvj2

items.title: [onnx] ONNX: Denial of service via unchecked expansion of packed sub-byte tensors in ONNX Python APIs
items.summary: SummaryONNX's Python tensor-materialization helpers could allocate memory according to attacker-controlled tensor dimensions without verifying that a packed sub-byte payload contained the declared number of elements.A very small model could therefore cause a disproportionately large allocation when an application called onnx.numpy_helper.to_array() or constructed onnx.reference.ReferenceEvaluator with the model. The issue affected UINT2, INT2, UINT4, INT4, and FLOAT4E2M1 tensors stored in either raw_data or packed int32_data.Technical detailsThe vulnerable _unpack_2bit() and _unpack_4bit() paths first allocated a small array based on the available packed bytes, then resized it to the shape declared in TensorProto.dims. They did not first confirm that the payload encoded enough logical elements for that shape.For example, the reporter demonstrated a 66-byte model containing one packed byte and a declared dimension of 700,000,000. The model passed onnx.checker.check_model() and allocated approximately 700 MB while materializing the initializer, followed by another large allocation when executing the reference evaluator.Loading, checking, or running shape inference on the serialized model alone did not trigger the allocation. The vulnerable tensor had to be materialized.ImpactAn application that materializes packed tensors from an untrusted model can exhaust available memory, causing denial of service. Memory corruption and code execution were not demonstrated.Affected versionsAffected: ONNX through 1.21.0Patched: ONNX 1.22.0RemediationUpgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.The primary fix validates the logical element count before resizing the unpacked NumPy array. A complementary checker change rejects an undersized packed payload before materialization.Materialization fix: onnx/onnx#8033Checker defense-in-depth: onnx/onnx#8038The five affected tensor types and both storage formats were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and are rejected before the oversized allocation.To verify the behavior using a released vulnerable package in an isolated environment, install onnx==1.21.0 with python -m pip install "onnx==1.21.0". Run memory-exhaustion demonstrations only with an appropriate process memory limit.SeverityThe vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.Referenceshttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/security/advisories/GHSA-q69g-f4f5-v8m7https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115922https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8033https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8038https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8066https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/05c1bc3bceceb8d3cf11e9e7fc7f19f971c44988https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/8de2cf6aa47928e6515ac6d9e1a8b4758886a7dfhttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/dce5876d6cc6cc30157af7d26a752ef44976da8ehttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/releases/tag/v1.22.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q69g-f4f5-v8m7

items.title: [onnx] ONNX: Null Pointer Dereference in ScanInferenceFunction Due to Missing Required Attribute
items.summary: SummaryONNX shape inference did not safely validate the required Scan num_scan_inputs attribute. Two malformed values could terminate or disrupt the process:If the attribute was missing, ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs") returned null and was dereferenced.If the attribute was negative, conversion to size_t produced a very large value that reached a vector allocation and raised std::length_error.The negative-value variant passed onnx.checker.check_model() before reaching shape inference.Technical detailsThe vulnerable Scan inference implementations used the following pattern:auto num_scan_inputs =    narrow_cast<size_t>(ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")->i());This code neither checked the returned pointer nor rejected a negative signed value before converting it to an unsigned size. The pattern was present in the current Scan inference function and the older opset 8 and 9 paths.The fix uses the required-attribute helper and checked narrowing:auto num_scan_inputs =    narrow<size_t>(getRequiredAttributeInt(ctx, "num_scan_inputs"));ImpactAn application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated or forced into an exceptional allocation path, causing denial of service. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.Affected versionsAffected: ONNX 1.4.0 through 1.21.0Patched: ONNX 1.22.0ONNX 1.4.0 is the first release containing the vulnerable Scan shape-inference implementation.RemediationUpgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.Fix: onnx/onnx#7916Commit: dd6bc92eaBoth reported models were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raise InferenceError.SeverityThe vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.The two triggers remain in one advisory because they affect the same required attribute, share the same unsafe conversion path and remediation, and were fixed in the same release.Referenceshttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/security/advisories/GHSA-m4pr-6v3c-6fgrhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115921https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7916https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/dd6bc92ea39fd2274fd671f0734b0b8b558356f5https://github.com/onnx/onnx/releases/tag/v1.22.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4pr-6v3c-6fgr

items.title: [onnx] ONNX: Out-of-Bounds Read in RNN/GRU/LSTM Shape Inference (Old Opsets, Missing Rank Check)
items.summary: SummaryONNX shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when processing a malformed RNN, GRU, or LSTM node from opsets 1–6 whose first input had a rank other than three.RNNShapeInference_opset1_to_6() checked whether the input shape was present but accessed dim(0) and dim(1) without first checking its rank. A crafted model could therefore terminate a process that called onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes(). The model passed onnx.checker.check_model() before reaching the vulnerable path.Technical detailsThe vulnerable code read dimensions unconditionally:if (hasInputShape(ctx, 0)) {  const auto& first_input_shape = getInputShape(ctx, 0);  seq_length = first_input_shape.dim(0);  batch_size = first_input_shape.dim(1);}For an undersized shape, protobuf's repeated-field access read outside the intended array in release builds. The observed result was SIGSEGV; sanitizer and debug builds terminated on a protobuf bounds check.The newer opset 7–13 and opset 14+ inference paths already required the first input to have rank three and were not affected.ImpactAn application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. Exploitation does not require privileges or human interaction once the model is processed. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.Affected versionsAffected: ONNX through 1.21.0Patched: ONNX 1.22.0The vulnerable schemas are limited to RNN and LSTM opsets 1–6 and GRU opsets 3–6.RemediationUpgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix validates that the first input has rank three before accessing its dimensions.Fix: onnx/onnx#7879Commit: 92e541266The original malformed model was also re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises InferenceError.SeverityThe vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.Referenceshttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/security/advisories/GHSA-48m4-24cq-37qfhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115919https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7879https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/92e541266af5dd38cfa48aeb92206f4268a066cdhttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/releases/tag/v1.22.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-48m4-24cq-37qf

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Permissive default CORS origins allow cross-origin requests to the vLLM HTTP server
items.summary: SummaryThe OpenAI-compatible server registers Starlette CORSMiddleware withallowed_origins defaulting to ["*"], and performs no authentication unless--api-key (or VLLM_API_KEY) is configured. A web page on any origin can sendrequests to a vLLM server that the victim's browser can reach (for examplelocalhost or an internal/VPN address) and read the responses. The defaultallow_credentials=False blocks cookie-bearing cross-origin requests; becausevLLM authenticates with a bearer header rather than cookies, the wildcard stillpermits untokenized access to an unauthenticated server and read access when thecaller already holds a token.DetailsAffected componentsvllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py - allowed_origins default value.vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py - CORSMiddlewareregistration.vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py - auth middleware and itsguarded path prefixes. Root causevllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py:allow_credentials: bool = False"""Allow credentials."""allowed_origins: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: ["*"])"""Allowed origins."""vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py:app.add_middleware(    CORSMiddleware,    allow_origins=args.allowed_origins,    allow_credentials=args.allow_credentials,    allow_methods=args.allowed_methods,    allow_headers=args.allowed_headers,)The auth middleware is added only when a token is configured and guards only the/v1, /v2, /inference, and /cohere prefixes. /v1/load_lora_adapter and/v1/unload_lora_adapter are inside /v1 and therefore do require a key whenone is set; they are open only when no key is configured and dynamic LoRAupdating is enabled.ImpactA malicious page can enumerate models (GET /v1/models), issuePOST /v1/chat/completions, consume GPU time, and read model output throughthe victim's browser.When the server is reachable only from the victim's network, the browser actsas a proxy a remote website could not otherwise use.With allow_credentials=False, cookie-based CSRF does not apply; the exposureis cross-origin request execution and response disclosure.This advisory was fixed in MR61009.Referenceshttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-vvpg-rrww-wpmhhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115917https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61009https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fcae5c98870ff2c20659731dce7ba3a3ff0d48aahttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vvpg-rrww-wpmh

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Phi-4 multimodal audio encoder materializes and retains full attention matrices: a single max-length audio OOM-crashes the vLLM engine
items.summary: SummaryThe Phi-4 multimodal audio encoder (phi4mm_audio.py / phi4mm_utils.py) runs its conformer attention in eager mode by default: the official HF config of microsoft/Phi-4-multimodal-instruct does not set use_pt_scaled_dot_product_attention, so the default False applies (phi4mm_audio.py:166, :876; phi4mm_utils.py:1669). The eager path fully materializes the attention probability matrix of shape [n_chunks, 16, 500, 500] per layer — and then stores it on the module: self.attn = attn (phi4mm_utils.py:1802, a torch.jit.Attribute declared at :1693), keeping a live reference for every one of the 24 encoder layers.The only gates on audio length are the server-side limits VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=25 and VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=600 (envs.py:83-84) — i.e. a 10-minute clip is a legal input by default. A 600 s clip becomes 60,000 mel frames, which the encoder unfolds into 500-frame chunks (phi4mm_audio.py:996, max_seq_len = 500), giving n_chunks ≈ 120. Each layer therefore materializes a 120×16×500×500 matrix (1–2 GiB depending on dtype), and the module attribute keeps all completed layers' matrices alive, so GPU memory climbs monotonically within a single request until an allocation fails.Verified end-to-end on the official vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0 image: one 19.2 MB silent 600 s WAV → worker torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.29 GiB ... 501.75 MiB free ... 22.09 GiB allocated by PyTorch inside get_audio_features (phi4mm_audio.py:1279 → :1332 → phi4mm_utils.py:1386) → EngineCore encountered a fatal error → API EngineDeadError → whole server down; /health refuses connections. Total time from request to dead service: ~6 seconds.A secondary effect: because self.attn persists on the module after the request ends, the matrices of the last audio request stay resident indefinitely (observed +50 MiB pinned after a single 5 s control request); they are only overwritten by the next audio request, so the resident footprint equals the largest audio processed since startup.Details1. Root cause. MultiHeadedAttention.forward_attention in eager mode computes attn = masked_softmax(scores, mask) and unconditionally executes self.attn = attn (phi4mm_utils.py:1795-1802). The attribute is a leftover inference/debug hook (used by torch.jit.Attribute(None, Tensor | None) at :1693); in serving it serves no purpose but pins the full [batch·chunks, heads, T, T] tensor per layer past both the layer's forward and the request's lifetime. The SDP attention branch (use_pt_scaled_dot_product_attention=True) never materializes this matrix — but the HF config does not enable it and the code default is False.2. Why one request suffices. The conformer chunks long audio to max_seq_len = 500 frames (phi4mm_audio.py:996). Duration is bounded only by VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=600, so n_chunks reaches ~120 for a maximal clip. With 16 heads and fp32 scores, one layer's attention tensor is ~1.8 GiB (the observed failing allocation was 2.29 GiB, consistent with the scores+bias materialization). The encoder has num_blocks=24, attention_heads=16, attention_dim=1024, time_reduction=8 (HF config). Weights plus a handful of retained per-layer matrices exhaust the ~2.3 GiB headroom that --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 leaves on a 24 GB card — mid-forward, on the first request.4. Deployment reality. --trust-remote-code is the documented, standard way to serve this model (the HF model card instructs it), so the finding applies to default deployments. The crash is deterministic, not load-dependent: scheduler stats at death show a single running request and near-zero KV cache usage.ImpactAny unauthenticated client that can reach the chat/completions API of a default deployment serving Phi-4-multimodal-instruct (or any model reusing this audio tower) can kill the entire engine with one request carrying a perfectly legal 10-minute audio clip (silent noise suffices — no crafted content needed). Full denial of service, requiring a process restart. On GPUs with more headroom (e.g. 80 GB at default utilization) a single request may survive, but the eager path still materializes GiB-scale per-layer matrices and retains the last request's tensors indefinitely, so a few sequential max-length requests — or normal traffic following one — achieve the same result.Relation to prior art: the only public Phi-4-mm advisory we found, GHSA-vc6m-hm49-g9qg, concerns a CPU-side quadratic-cost path — different subsystem, different mechanism. GitHub search for "phi4mm audio OOM/memory" (31 results, 2026-10-08) shows no report of this attention-retention issue; main (2026-10-08) is unchanged.Suggested remediation (any one breaks the chain; 1+2 recommended):Remove self.attn = attn from the serving path (or gate it behind an explicit debug/output_attentions flag) so attention matrices are freed when the layer returns.Default use_pt_scaled_dot_product_attention to True (flash/SDPA kernels never materialize the [B, H, T, T] matrix); keep eager only

items.title: [vllm] vLLM DeepSeek-OCR image processing vulnerable to denial of service
items.summary: SummaryAny vLLM deployment serving a model of the DeepSeek-OCR family — deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR-2, or baidu/Unlimited-OCR (whose UnlimitedOCRForCausalLM subclasses DeepseekOCRForCausalLM) — can be killed by a single unauthenticated chat request carrying an ordinary, schema-valid PNG image, under completely default server configuration.The image model's input validation contains a guard inherited from the upstream DeepSeek-OCR reference implementation:# vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_ocr.py:478-479  (_parse_and_validate_image_input)if torch.sum(pixel_values).item() == 0:    return NoneIn the original research code this was an empty-batch shortcut; in vLLM's serving architecture pixel_values is the actual client image tensor, and the condition is exactly satisfiable by a legitimate image: the in-tree DeepseekOCRProcessor normalizes pixels with ToTensor + Normalize(0.5, 0.5) (vllm/transformers_utils/processors/deepseek_ocr.py:120-140), mapping pixel value 0 → exactly −1.0 and 255 → exactly +1.0 in float32. A 1024×1024 image that is half pure black and half pure white (a perfectly ordinary 1-bit-style scanned-document PNG for an OCR model) therefore yields torch.sum(pixel_values) == 0.0 exactly (equal counts of ±1.0; pairwise reduction stays integer-exact, well inside float32's 2²⁴ exactness bound). ImageOps.pad(image, (1024, 1024)) is the identity map for an already-1024×1024 image (processors/deepseek_ocr.py:350-355), so no padding pixels disturb the balance.Returning None makes embed_multimodal return None (deepseek_ocr.py:606-611), which immediately trips the engine-side sanity check in the worker:# vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:512  (sanity_check_mm_encoder_outputs)assert isinstance(mm_embeddings, (list, tuple, torch.Tensor)), (    "Expected multimodal embeddings to be a list/tuple of 2D tensors, ...")The AssertionError is raised inside the encoder runner of the EngineCore worker process with no per-request containment, escapes to the busy loop's top-level handler (vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1368, "EngineCore encountered a fatal error."), triggers EngineDeadError at the API server (vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:843), and the whole process tree shuts down permanently. /health refuses connections until a manual restart.Verified end-to-end on the official vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0 image (id d076d77d8dad) with real deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR weights: after confirming /health 200, a text chat 200, and two control images (all-white and all-black 1024×1024) 200, the single half-black/half-white request returned HTTP 500 (EngineCore encountered an issue), the engine log shows AssertionError: Expected multimodal embeddings to be a list/tuple of 2D tensors ... got <class 'NoneType'> at v1/worker/utils.py:512, the API server shut itself down, and the container exited (Exited (0), OOMKilled=false). Every subsequent request, including GET /health, fails at the socket. The vulnerable check is unchanged on main (verified 2026-09-30 against the raw file on the default branch).Environment notes (disclosed for completeness; unrelated to the sink): (1) the v0.30.0 image's Triton version refuses to compile deepencoder.py's fused rel-pos attention kernel (LOG2E non-constexpr global) during the startup profile run; per the compiler's own suggestion we set TRITON_ALLOW_NON_CONSTEXPR_GLOBALS=1 — an environment workaround only, no source file was modified. (2) DeepSeek-OCR ships no chat_template, so verification passed a one-line --chat-template that concatenates message content text; this does not touch the image data path. (3) The zero-sum check aggregates over the whole per-step modality batch, so the trigger image must be alone in its encoder batch — trivially true on an idle instance (our verification: first attempt, single request), and simply retried otherwise.Details1. The processor maps an ordinary binary image to exactly ±1.0 pixels. DeepseekOCRProcessor.tokenize_with_images (vllm/transformers_utils/processors/deepseek_ocr.py:338-389) builds the global view as ImageOps.pad(image, (base_size, base_size), color=mean*255) with base_size = 1024 (:21). For a 1024×1024 input the pad is a no-op (same-size ImageOps.contain resampling is the identity: the bicubic kernel passes through sample points exactly). ImageTransform (:120-140) then applies T.ToTensor() (uint8 0 → 0.0, 255 → 1.0, exact in float32) and T.Normalize((0.5,)*3, (0.5,)*3) (0.0 → −1.0, 1.0 → +1.0, exact). A left-half-black/right-half-white 1024×1024 RGB image therefore produces 1,572,864 elements of −1.0 and 1,572,864 of +1.0; torch.sum (pairwise/tree reduction, partial sums bounded by 1.58M ≪ 2²⁴) evaluates to exactly 0.0, and .item() == 0 is True. All of this runs in the API process and passes every validation layer: the image is 1 MP, far under the default VLLM_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS cap of 178,956,970 (vllm/envs.py:86).2. The zero guard turns a valid image into a None encoder output. _parse_and_validate_image_input (deepseek_ocr.py:468-497) returns

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Untrusted EPS inputs can trigger denial of service or Ghostscript RCE
items.summary: SummaryIn vLLM 0.30.0, ImageMediaIO passes attacker-controlled image bytes to Pillow's format autodetection without restricting the accepted formats; the request's MIME label does not constrain decoder selection. An EPS payload labeled image/png reached the host's Ghostscript executable. On a host with Ghostscript affected by CVE-2024-29510, this exposes the known Ghostscript sandbox escape through vLLM's image-loading path and can execute commands with the vLLM process's privileges. A bounded marker-command payload executed through the PyPI wheel's actual ImageMediaIO.load_base64() implementation using Debian Ghostscript 10.03.0. The loader-level execution is reproduced; the HTTP request path is source-traced but was not exercised end to end. This report concerns vLLM's untrusted-format dispatch and does not claim a new Ghostscript vulnerability. Exploitation requires an image-capable request path, a caller able to reach it under the deployment's authentication policy, and a vulnerable host Ghostscript build.DetailsImageMediaIO is the boundary where attacker-controlled bytes enter Pillow's format autodetection: the declared MIME type does not constrain decoder selection, and the loader calls Image.open(BytesIO(data)) without a Pillow format allowlist. Pillow recognizes EPS by its file signature, and vLLM's subsequent image.load() call enters Pillow's EPS processing path. The OpenAI chat multimodal parser reaches this path through parse_image() and fetch_image() and the media connector; the data URL path extracts the MIME label and forwards the bytes to the loader (source). This is the vLLM-specific issue: untrusted image bytes can select a Pillow-supported format parser. Each downstream impact depends on the relevant parser, component version, and host configuration.Pillow recognizes EPS by its file signature and invokes Ghostscript with -dSAFER, -sDEVICE=pnmraw, and the untrusted EPS input (Pillow EPS plugin, load path). The command execution in this report uses the already-known Ghostscript CVE-2024-29510, which allows crafted PostScript to bypass -dSAFER; Ghostscript lists 10.03.1 as the upstream fixed version (Ghostscript CVE details). This is an N-day dependency chain: CVE-2024-29510 provides the command-execution primitive, while the vLLM-specific issue is that untrusted, remotely supplied image bytes can reach the affected interpreter. No new Ghostscript flaw is claimed here.The vLLM Python requirements declare Pillow but not Ghostscript, so this execution chain depends on a Ghostscript executable supplied by the host or deployment image. I reproduced command execution with the PyPI vllm==0.30.0 wheel, Pillow 12.3.0, and Debian amd64 Ghostscript 10.03.0~dfsg-1. The Codean Labs CVE-2024-29510 testkit identified that Ghostscript build as vulnerable. The adapted EPS payload ran only touch on a temporary marker. The marker existed after the loader call, although Pillow then raised ValueError because the exploit changes Ghostscript's output device. The API route was traced in source but a model-backed HTTP request was not run. Only PyPI vllm==0.30.0 was checked; no wider affected release range or other Ghostscript vendor build is claimed.The same input boundary also exposes a separate Pillow-only denial-of-service condition when the installed Pillow version is 12.0.0–12.2.0. CVE-2026-59203 is triggered by a negative %%BeginBinary byte count and causes Pillow's EPS parser to loop during Image.open(); it does not invoke Ghostscript or provide code execution (Pillow advisory). The published vllm==0.30.0 requirements leave Pillow unpinned, so an existing environment can retain an affected Pillow version; the source at commit bc21cba9673cfc2256a2726b4bc32f062237cd35 requires pillow>=12.3.0. In an isolated local check with Pillow 12.2.0, the official sample hung through ImageMediaIO.load_bytes() and MediaConnector.fetch_image_async(). Eight concurrent image loads occupied the connector's eight media-loading threads and left a benign image load queued. Pillow 12.3.0 rejected the sample promptly. This confirms a conditional media-processing DoS path, separate from the Ghostscript RCE chain; full HTTP-server availability was not measured.ImpactWhen a vLLM image-processing endpoint accepts attacker-supplied content and the host has Ghostscript affected by CVE-2024-29510, a caller who can reach the endpoint can trigger command execution as the vLLM process user. API-key authentication and network access controls determine who can reach the request path. Deployments without Ghostscript or with a build fixed for CVE-2024-29510 are not affected by this execution chain. Separately, existing environments that run vLLM 0.30.0 with Pillow 12.0.0–12.2.0 are exposed to CVE-2026-59203 through the same image-format dispatch boundary; the demonstrated impact is exhaustion of media-loading workers, and this Pillow CVE does not cause RCE. The report asks vLLM to assess and address the unsafe dispatch of untrusted image bytes and

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Public multimodal SHM handle forgery reaches worker-side `pickle.loads()` with insecure serialization disabled
items.summary: AffectedEcosystem / package: pip / vllmAffected versions: vLLM < 0.32.0.SummaryWhen --mm-processor-cache-type shm is enabled, vLLM's multimodal SHM cache represents a cached item with an address and monotonic_id pair and treats that pair as authority to dereference shared memory in the worker. A public scale-out request can supply its own multimodal features.kwargs_data, so an authenticated caller can forge an inner SHM carrier that points at attacker-controlled bytes already staged in the ring buffer. The worker then reaches pickle.loads() while deserializing the forged object.This is reachable through ordinary public HTTP routes and does not require VLLM_ALLOW_INSECURE_SERIALIZATION=1. The live chain used /v1/chat/completions/render to obtain a valid feature envelope, /v1/chat/completions to stage attacker-chosen bytes into SHM, and /inference/v1/generate to submit the forged inner carrier.Affected codeLinks pinned to the confirmed commit 752a3a504485 (v0.25.1):vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_object_storage.py#L375-L400 — SHM object deserialization reaches pickle.loads(serialized_data) for byte objects.vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L567-L581 — sender emits an SHM carrier containing only address and monotonic_id.vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L711-L737 — worker dereferences the untrusted pair and reads the SHM object.vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py#L146-L173 — public features.kwargs_data is decoded into engine input without authenticating SHM handles before handoff.The public scale-out route decodes attacker-controlled features.kwargs_data into MultiModalKwargsItems and hands them straight to the engine — no authentication of the SHM handle:# vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py Lines 155-165            # Deserialize tensor data when present; None → cache hit.            mm_kwargs: dict[str, list[MultiModalKwargsItem | None]] = {}            if features.kwargs_data is not None:                for modality, items in features.kwargs_data.items():                    mm_kwargs[modality] = [                        decode_mm_kwargs_item(item) if item is not None else None                        for item in items                    ]            else:                for modality, hashes in features.mm_hashes.items():                    mm_kwargs[modality] = [None] * len(hashes)In the worker, a decoded item that carries an address is treated as authority to dereference shared memory: the (address, monotonic_id) pair alone drives the read, with no binding to the cache key or to who issued the handle:# vllm/multimodal/cache.py Lines 711-723    @override    def get_and_update_item(        self,        mm_item: MultiModalKwargsItem | None,        mm_hash: str,    ) -> MultiModalKwargsItem:        assert mm_item is not None, f"Expected an address item for {mm_hash=}"        if "address" in mm_item:            address = cast(int, mm_item["address"].data)            monotonic_id = cast(int, mm_item["monotonic_id"].data)            return self._shm_cache.get(address, monotonic_id)        return mm_itemThe dereference lands in the SHM deserializer, which pickle.loads() any chunk tagged as bytes — so attacker bytes staged in the ring buffer are unpickled in the worker process:# vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_object_storage.py Lines 375-400    def deserialize(self, data_view: memoryview) -> Any:        # pickle.loads do not read past the end of a pickled object        # within a large buffer, so we can skip storing the metadata size        type_name, nbytes, len_arr = pickle.loads(data_view)        serialized_data = data_view[-nbytes:]        if type_name == torch.Tensor.__name__:            obj = []            start_idx = 0            for length in len_arr:                item_bytes = serialized_data[start_idx : start_idx + length]                obj.append(item_bytes)                start_idx += length            obj = self.tensor_decoder.decode(obj)        elif type_name == self._mm_kwargs_item_cls.__name__:            obj = []            start_idx = 0            for length in len_arr:                item_bytes = serialized_data[start_idx : start_idx + length]                obj.append(item_bytes)                start_idx += length            obj = self.mm_decoder.decode(obj)        elif type_name == bytes.__name__:            obj = pickle.loads(serialized_data)        else:            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported object type '{type_name}' in metadata")        return objImpactAn ordinary authenticated inference caller can execute arbitrary Python in the worker process on a deployment that uses SHM multimodal caching. The live proof used a benign marker gadget and also caused the EngineCore health endpoint to fall from 200 to 503 after the forged request. The exploit is reachable with VLLM_ALLOW_INSECURE_SERIALIZATION=0; it abuses the built-in SHM object deserializer, not the separate optional msgpack ext-hook flag.Suggested FixAuthenticate every SHM carrier with a se

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Out-of-vocabulary prompt token id passes input validation and triggers a CUDA device-side assert (engine crash / DoS)
items.summary: For a model whose vocabulary size is an exact multiple of the embedding padding size (64) — e.g. any Llama-2-family model, vocab 32000 — a single request carrying a pre-tokenized prompt with token id equal to the vocab size (32000) passes vLLM's input-id validation but is one past the last embedding row. At tensor-parallel size 1 the embedding lookup does not mask indices, so the id reaches F.embedding out of range and raises a CUDA device-side assert, which poisons the engine's CUDA context and takes the engine down. Any client that can send pre-tokenized input (/v1/completions with prompt as token ids, /tokenize-fed flows, or the kv_transfer_params["prompt_token_ids"] reuse path) can trigger it.Root causevllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py accepts a token id when id <= max(tokenizer.max_token_id, model_config.get_vocab_size() - 1).vllm/tokenizers/hf.py computes max_token_id = max(max(vocab.values()), tokenizer.vocab_size). For Llama-2 tokenizers max(vocab.values()) = 31999 but tokenizer.vocab_size = 32000, so max_token_id = 32000 — one greater than the largest valid id.The engine bound therefore becomes max(32000, 31999) = 32000, and id 32000 is accepted.The model's embedding has pad_vocab_size(32000, 64) = 32000 rows (no padding), valid indices 0..31999. At VocabParallelEmbedding.forward with tp_size == 1 there is no masking, so index 32000 hits F.embedding out of range.Affectedtp=1 (single GPU per model — common per-copy layout). tp>1 masks via get_masked_input_and_mask, so the id is clamped, not an OOB — likely wrong output rather than a crash.Models whose vocab is a multiple of 64 with tokenizer.vocab_size one past the max real id (Llama-2 family, vocab 32000, is the clear case). Qwen2.5 is NOT affected (padded headroom).Suggested fixmax_token_id in vllm/tokenizers/hf.py now uses tokenizer.vocab_size - 1, so an id equal to the vocabulary size fails input validation instead of reaching the embedding. Fixed in MR59491, released in v0.32.0.ReporterShijie Lyu (GitHub shijie-lyu lshjhf@gmail.com). Reported privately per SECURITY.This advisory was fixed in MR59491.Referenceshttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115916https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59491https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/37cecc8141e2dcba9dd534897a164d4baaf27229https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Responses API bypasses trust_request_chat_template for chat_template_kwargs
items.summary: SummaryvLLM's /v1/responses endpoint accepts request-level chat_template_kwargs, but does not apply the --trust-request-chat-template gate that protects Chat Completions, render, tokenize, and pooling paths.When the server is run with the documented default trust_request_chat_template=False and no explicit --chat-template, a Responses request can pass:{"chat_template_kwargs": {"chat_template": "<attacker Jinja template>"}}That key is preserved by ChatParams.get_apply_chat_template_kwargs() and then bound as the chat_template parameter to the shared HF renderer. Prior vLLM advisories establish that request-controlled Jinja chat templates can cause CPU/memory exhaustion. This report covers the current-head Responses sibling path missed by the earlier fixes.Technical DetailsThe shared OpenAI frontend has a validation helper that rejects request-supplied chat templates unless the trust flag is enabled. It explicitly checks both top-level chat_template and chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"].Responses is a separate serving path:vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/protocol.py exposes chat_template_kwargs.ResponsesRequest.build_chat_params() merges request kwargs.OpenAIServingResponses._effective_chat_template_kwargs() uses those kwargs.ChatParams.get_apply_chat_template_kwargs() preserves a request chat_template key when the server chat template is None.vllm/renderers/hf.py unpacks the result into safe_apply_chat_template.There is no equivalent trust gate in vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/serving.py.ImpactAn authenticated caller who can submit /v1/responses requests can supply a request-controlled Jinja chat template despite the trust flag being disabled. The expected fixed behavior is the same as Chat Completions: reject chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"] unless the server was started with --trust-request-chat-template.Suggested FixAdd trust_request_chat_template to OpenAIServingResponses.Pass args.trust_request_chat_template when constructing the Responses serving object.Reject request.chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"] before rendering when trust is false.Keep ordinary kwargs such as enable_thinking working.Add regression tests for default-deny and opt-in-allow behavior on /v1/responses.Affected Package/VersionsSource sweep found the affected shape in:v0.16.0v0.18.0v0.20.0v0.21.0v0.22.0v0.22.1v0.23.0current checkout 470229c37efaf69c86e8bc97482b0b1ff7551c65current origin/main b3f0a0a0df76dda92ec4b2c9335f77e84adad911Suggested affected range:>= 0.16.0, <= 0.23.0Appendix: Duplicate ResearchThis is related to, but distinct from:GHSA-6fvq-23cw-5628 / CVE-2025-61620GHSA-69j4-grxj-j64p / CVE-2025-62426Those advisories establish the security impact of request-controlled Jinja templates and chat_template_kwargs, but they cover older Chat Completions/tokenize implementations. This report covers a current /v1/responses sibling path that still lacks the trust gate.Local prior submissions this report..029 do not cover this root cause.This advisory was fixed in MR50300.Referenceshttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-x567-49g5-p4cfhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115918https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50300https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/cff08b461e086523cee8bba5bd3c66d302625134https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x567-49g5-p4cf

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: DoS via unbounded chat_template Jinja2 rendering exhausts the renderer thread pool
items.summary: SummaryvLLM renders chat templates by passing the resolved Jinja2 source to tokenizer.apply_chat_template(), which compiles and .render()s it in an ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment. The sandbox prevents code-execution escapes but imposes no wall-clock timeout, no output-size cap, and no nested-loop or binop limit. The render runs in a ThreadPoolExecutor whose max_workers defaults to 1, and CPython worker threads cannot be interrupted. An authenticated API client (or a malicious model repo loaded with trust_remote_code=False) can therefore submit a single short template and permanently wedge all chat-style endpoints (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, /tokenize, /pooling-chat, /invocations-chat) for every tenant until the process is restarted. A string-multiplication variant instead OOM-kills the API-server process. Because of a separately-reported (GHSA-jmjw-q4x3-hmc2) gate omission on /v1/responses, the remote authenticated attacker vector works in default vllm serve configuration with no operator opt-in.ImpactA single authenticated request of <100 bytes permanently denies all chat-style inference (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, /tokenize, /pooling-chat, /invocations-chat) to every tenant of the API-server replica until the operator restarts the process. The string-multiplication variant OOM-kills the process. In a multi-tenant deployment this is a cross-tenant denial-of-service from any one tenant. From the malicious-model angle, a model repo whose tokenizer_config.json carries the hostile template wedges every replica that loads it on the first legitimate chat request, with trust_remote_code=False.Preconditions: any non-harmony model (model_type != gpt_oss); renderer_num_workers at its default of 1; for the default-config authenticated API attacker vector, --chat-template must be unset (the default because most HF models ship their own).Blast radius: API-server process, per replica. Engine/worker processes unaffected by the CPU variant (event loop survives); affected by the memory variant (process OOM).Persistence: until process restart. Survives client disconnect.This advisory was fixed in MR50300.Referenceshttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-542m-9234-8gvfhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115911https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50300https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/cff08b461e086523cee8bba5bd3c66d302625134https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-542m-9234-8gvf

items.title: [langgraph-cli] LangGraph CLI prints the registry push token in `langgraph deploy --verbose` output
items.summary: Summarylanggraph deploy --verbose printed the temporary registry push token that the CLI uses to log Docker in to the deployment's image registry. Anyone who could read that output, for example in CI logs, could use the token until it expired.DetailsWhen Docker is available, langgraph deploy builds the image locally, requests a push token from LangSmith, and runs docker login --password-stdin with the token on stdin. The CLI's subprocess helper printed each command's stdin when verbose output was on, and the login step inherited --verbose, so the token was printed right after the docker login command line.langgraph-cli 0.4.15 through 0.4.31 are affected. Starting with 0.4.32, the login step runs without verbose output. Deploys run without --verbose, and deploys that build the image remotely, never printed the token.ImpactYou may be affected if you ran langgraph deploy --verbose with an affected version and the output was kept or shared, for example in CI logs or terminal recordings. The token is short-lived (at most 12 hours) and limited to that deployment's image repository. Someone holding it before it expired could pull the deployment's images and push new images to that repository. Deployments reference their image by digest, so a pushed image does not run unless the deployment is updated to use it, which requires a LangSmith API key with access to the deployment.RemediationUpgrade to langgraph-cli 0.4.32 or later. 0.4.37 also stops --verbose from printing the input of any command the CLI runs. Tokens printed more than 12 hours ago have expired.Referenceshttps://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/security/advisories/GHSA-8prr-f582-jqq3https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115885https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/8482https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/commit/1afaca35a0d4962fb0203a0e9133a07ffd6a553chttps://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/releases/tag/cli%3D%3D0.4.32.dev0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8prr-f582-jqq3

items.title: [autobahn] Autobahn Python: permessage-brotli inflates a whole frame before maxMessagePayloadSize is checked (incomplete fix of GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566)
items.summary: Summarypermessage-brotli inflates each frame fully before checking maxMessagePayloadSize, so one 421-byte frame makes the server allocate about 545 MiB even with a 1 MiB message limit (brotli expands about 1,000,000:1). Any unauthenticated client can exhaust server memory this way on servers that enable permessage-brotli. This bypasses the GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 fix.DetailsIn 26.7.1 the receive path passes the remaining maxMessagePayloadSize budget to decompress_message_data(..., max_output_len=...). deflate and bzip2 stop at that budget. PerMessageBrotli.decompress_message_data (compress_brotli.py) instead calls self._decompressor.process(data) with no limit and compares the length afterwards, so the whole frame is inflated first.The code comment and changelog say this is still "bounded on the wire by maxFramePayloadSize", but brotli reaches about 1,000,000:1 (841 bytes inflate to 1 GiB), so that bound means little. A 421-byte frame against a 1 MiB budget peaks at 545 MiB before the 1009 rejection.An autobahn asyncio server on 127.0.0.1 accepting permessage-brotli, with maxFramePayloadSize=64 KiB and maxMessagePayloadSize=1 MiB, received one small brotli frame from an autobahn client and peaked at 545 MiB (baseline 28 MiB). A few concurrent connections can exhaust memory.brotli ≥ 1.2.0 has Decompressor.process(data, output_buffer_limit=N), so the backend can stop at max_output_len like deflate and bzip2 (and the extra's floor can be raised to brotli>=1.2.0).Tested on autobahn 26.7.1 (latest) with brotli 1.2.0; compress_brotli.py on master is unchanged. This affects servers that enable permessage-brotli (opt-in, needs the compress extra).Proof of conceptHow to run the PoCpython3 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activatepip install autobahn==26.7.1 brotli==1.2.0python3 poc_autobahn.py# PoC: autobahn 26.7.1 permessage-brotli inflates a whole frame before maxMessagePayloadSize is checked.import brotli, resourcefrom autobahn.websocket.compress import PerMessageBrotlic = brotli.Compressor()  # build a 256 MiB-of-zeros frame without holding the plaintextframe = b"".join(c.process(b"\0" * (1 << 20)) for _ in range(256)) + c.finish()pmce = PerMessageBrotli(is_server=True, server_no_context_takeover=False, client_no_context_takeover=False)pmce.start_decompress_message()print(len(frame), "bytes on the wire; peak RSS before:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB")try:    pmce.decompress_message_data(frame, max_output_len=1 << 20)  # remaining budget: 1 MiBexcept Exception as e:    print(type(e).__name__, "| peak RSS after:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB")Output:421 bytes on the wire; peak RSS before: 36 MiBPayloadExceededError | peak RSS after: 545 MiBImpactAn unauthenticated WebSocket client can make a server that enabled permessage-brotli allocate hundreds of MB or more per tiny frame, regardless of the configured maxMessagePayloadSize. That is the memory-exhaustion DoS GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 was meant to prevent.Credit goes to Adrian Korwel.Referenceshttps://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-python/security/advisories/GHSA-pjh6-c8mg-3x7mhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116579https://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-python/pull/1987https://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-python/commit/a41442bbee4f6126a8ce1bb892840124c24d16f1https://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-python/releases/tag/v26_10_1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pjh6-c8mg-3x7m
